I always wondered why Godot didn’t offer fully baked lighting like Unity and Unreal; I eventually just convinced myself that it was entirely obsolete...

On the other hand, do you think it’s worth breaking compatibility in favor of better names for these static modes? I think having 'static' and 'static baked' is very confusing. We could change them to something more familiar, like Unity’s style (Mixed and Baked) or Unreal’s (Static and Stationary). I’m also open to it if anyone has a different proposal.

> On the other hand, do you think it’s worth breaking compatibility in favor of better names for these static modes? I think having 'static' and 'static baked' is very confusing. We could change them to something more familiar, like Unity’s style (Mixed and Baked) or Unreal’s (Static and Stationary). I’m also open to it if anyone has a different proposal.

My suggestion would be 'static' and 'inert'.

@LiveTrower @Stwend I've been thinking about changing the names too but I have no idea who would have the authority to make a decision like that.  Also, we would need to agree on what the new names would be.  I'm only familiar with the baked lightmap system, so I don't really know how these modes work in VoxelGI or SDFGI.

From my perspective "Dynamic" never made sense because it sounds like you can move the light, but if you move the light it will leave it's bounced light behind.

Right now we have:

Disabled  (this makes perfect sense)
Static  (baked onto static geo but is real time on dynamic objects)
Dynamic  (baked indirect, real time direct, misleading IMO.  I think this was called Mixed in Unity)
Static Baked  (the full monty, actually static, fully baked)

I also would rather they were ordered from least backed to most baked in the drop down list.  Right now it's kinda up and down.

Does anyone have a set of suggestions?  I'll give it a go

Disabled
Baked Direct
Baked Indirect
Fully Baked

Maybe we could drop the word Baked on all of them because it's already a Bake Mode.  Also, reorder?

> @LiveTrower @Stwend I've been thinking about changing the names too but I have no idea who would have the authority to make a decision like that. Also, we would need to agree on what the new names would be. I'm only familiar with the baked lightmap system, so I don't really know how these modes work in VoxelGI or SDFGI.

According to the [documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_light3d.html#enum-light3d-bakemode), Disabled mode deactivates GI, but it doesn't specify which GI methods it affects. Dynamic mode is only intended for SDFGI and VoxelGI, while Static mode is for LightmapGI, SDFGI, and VoxelGI.

I ran some tests to see how each one behaves, and in practice, it is completely different:

**Disabled:** It seems to be the only one that works correctly across SDFGI, VoxelGI, and LightmapGI.

**Dynamic:** This makes sense for SDFGI and VoxelGI since indirect lighting is calculated in real-time, but it doesn't make sense for LightmapGI because only the indirect lighting is static.

**Static:** This makes no sense for VoxelGI because there is no effect at all, even though the documentation claims there is (possible bug). Regarding SDFGI, I'm not entirely sure since Static and Disabled modes behave the same (possible bug). For LightmapGI, it does make sense because both indirect and direct lighting are calculated.

In my opinion, we should add one more mode besides Fully Baked:

- Disabled
- Dynamic
- Baked Indirect
- Baked Mixed (Direct + Indirect)
- Fully Baked

> @LiveTrower Thanks for doing this. From what you say it sounds like the bake modes barely work in SDFGI and VoxelGI, which is unfortunate, but fixing bugs in those modes is obviously beyond this PR.
> 
> I disagree about Dynamic not making sense in LightmapGI . This can be a main use case for the main light in your scene. Take an indoor dark cave scene lit only by one beam of light coming down through a large hole in the ceiling. The bounced light illuminates the walls, but it doesn't need to be super accurate. You still want your main character to cast a shadow when standing in the actually light beam, and to receive proper real time light from it. This is what a "Dynamic" light can be used for in LightmapGI. Misnamed, but useful.

The thing is, we are talking about indirect lighting at the light source, and since it isn't being calculated in real-time within the lightmap, the light can no longer be considered dynamic. To avoid confusion, it would be best to place it in a different category.

> 
> As for your list of options. Is your intention to split Dynamic into two different modes? That would be more work and I don't see why it would be part of this PR. I guess the problem is that "Baked Indirect" doesn't describe the behavior in SDFGI and VoxelGI? I see that is a problem hmm.

Yea the issue is: how are light sources in static mode supposed to work when using VoxelGI or SDFGI?
@zomby138 The documentation also needs to be updated to clarify things as much as possible, but I’m not sure if you’re supposed to do that for this PR too.
For now I am going to leave it like this: If we decide to change the names it can be a new proposal. Unless anyone has anything else to suggest?

I think this PR is mixing too many concepts together. 

At it's core, it is doing two distinct things:
1. Baking direct lighting into probes
2. Disabling lights that have been baked

IMO by conflating these two distinct features I think this mode ends up being more controversial than it otherwise would be. 

### Baking direct lighting into probes

I haven't seen any proposals for this behaviour or any discussion of it. But it sounds like a cool idea to me. My gut feeling is that it may be better suited as property of LightmapGI itself instead of a per-node property. But I'm not sure since there hasn't really been any discussion about this.

Ultimately, a lot more work needs to be done to make probes sufficient for direct lighting. We don't do any de-ringing on the probes and if you use them for direct lighting you will need de-ringing except in very trivial cases. Further L2 just doesn't have enough resolution to capture the lighting info nicely. So the baked result is always going to feel like something out of an old PS2 game. Which could be fine for retro games! But we need to understand and be clear on what the reasoning is and what the goal is. 

### Disabling lights that have been baked

The current workflow in Godot for this is to use render layers. Put your dynamic objects on one render layer and your static objects on another. For fully baked lights you just exclude the dynamic objects using the cull_mask by turning off the dynamic object render layer in that lights cull mask. That way Godot will automatically cull those lights early in the rendering process. 

The beauty of using render layers is it provides way more flexibility than this PR plus it is way faster since it disables the lights at the culling phase instead of paying the full cost of culling and pairing before disabling the light (like this PR does).

Personally, my gut feeling is that the support for https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8040 comes more from misunderstanding render layers than it does from an actual need for this.

@clayjohn Hi John, let me try to put some of your concerns to rest.  First of all, I agree with you that the PR does those 2 things, but I would argue that either one is of no use without the other.

I am surprised to hear that you think the PR is controversial.  It has been in discussion for 2 and a half years now, and your post is the first whiff of controversy that it has seen.  One thing that HAS seen controversy is the lake of this feature, as you can see in this post: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8040#issuecomment-4148176713

You say "Baking direct lighting into probes: I haven't seen any proposals for this behavior or any discussion of it."  Yet you have linked the proposal that does exactly that in your post.

Your suggestion that it could be a LightmapGI property instead of a per Light property could be valid.  You'd need to put a case for it forward.  I assume you would have it bake all lights that are set to "Static" Baked Mode into the probes?  It would be less flexible.  But then wouldn't you agree that those lights would then all need to be culled for all objects no matter what the culling masks are set to?

The is only one set of SH probes, not one per render layer.  Maybe this is something you didn't consider?

The question of quality of direct light being stored in spherical harmonic L2 data was discussed briefly here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8040#issuecomment-4115065918

Playstation 2 style graphics are extremely popular among indie devs right now.  That is one of the two main use cases for this.  The other being when a level designer wants to make a room a little lighter, so they add a dull light to a room, set it to baked with a high bounce boost and use it as a sort of local ambient light.  Currently, doing this in Godot is a mess because you either end up with a real time light being rendered, sucking up performance, or inconsistent light levels between the static geo and dynamic.

As for your performance concerns, I direct you to @Calinou's benchmark tests here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8040#issuecomment-4329366190

And I encourage you to do your own benchmark too.  Please!

This PR disables the lights at the same level that culling layers does, or deeper.  You do not pay the cost of pairing.

Just adding my support over here, I'm now using this PR in my custom fork and so far it's working great for me and the art style in my game. Being able to bake the direct light into the probes is great :)
